newsitem.title: UK: Mark to find little joy as economy stumbles along.
newsitem.headline: Mark to find little joy as economy stumbles along.

text.p: Reeling from the dollar's latest surge, the mark is set to remain in the doldrums against other European currencies as Germany's economy continues to stumble along its bumpy path to recovery, analysts said on Tuesday.

German economic growth rebounded during the second quarter but recent economic data have been giving contradictory signals: weak industrial output and manufacturing orders on the one hand, buoyant business sentiment on the other.

"In Germany, we are looking at what can be termed a bumpy recovery at best," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "The economic outlook should keep the mark soft against the dollar and its European crosses."

Latest output data for October, released on Tuesday, showed pan-German industrial output down 1.8 percent on the month and west-German output falling 1.7 percent. After September's decline, the markets had bet on an improvement.

Speculation about a further cut in German interest rates is divided, however, after the Bundesbank eased the securities repurchase rate by a much larger-than-expected 30 basis points to 3.0 percent last August.

But expectations German monetary policy might be close to a turning point are far-fetched, analysts said. The Bundesbank is likely to be very concerned to avoid a mark resurgence which would hurt German exporters.

"I don't buy the story of another German rate cut but there's no reason to become concerned about monetary tightening so soon either," said Rainer Siegelkow, senior economist at West-LB in Duesseldorf.

The Bundesbank on Tuesday declined to comment directly on a bout of renewed rate cut speculation, but pointed to earlier comments by its president Hans Tietmeyer that rates would remain steady in the short term.
A monetary tightening would only be likely soon if inflation were to accelerate quickly, which looks unlikely at present.

Therefore, the name of the game for the mark is rangebound trading, barring a few hiccups here and there. Given the recent surge of most European high-yielders there might be room for an equally sharp correction initially before the mark settles into steadier territory.
Mark/lira, for example, is trading at 2 1/2 year lows around 980 lire, well below the central rate of 990 at which the lira re-joined the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) last week.
The British pound surged nearly four pfennigs overnight to 2.6370, its highest level since leaving the ERM in September 1992, but quickly reversed most of those gains.

The mark/French franc rate, the pillar of the quest to European monetary union in 1999, has already settled back after recent jitters over devaluation calls and the long-standing franc fort policy eased.
"There is very little reason to buy marks but some of the excessive selling we have seen this year is unlikely to be repeated," said a senior trader at a German bank in London.

Third quarter German gross domestic product data, due on Wednesday, are expected to show a rise of 0.9 percent from the previous quarter after 1.5 percent previously, with exports seen as the main driving force. Neither consumer nor investment spending will have contributed much, analysts said.
No improvement on the jobless front is expected from November unemployment data, due on Thursday. The total number of Germans out of work is likely to remain close to four million.
A positive for the mark, however, might come from progress on the stability pact to ensure fiscal stability in EMU.

European Union finance ministers on Monday agreed on the size of fines to be imposed on countries running excessive budget deficits. But they failed to agree on the level of economic weakness that would allow single currency members to escape penalties.
Ministers will meet again next week to try and reach agreement ahead of the Dublin EU summit on December 13.

"Dublin and the stability pact could put a spanner in the weak mark works," said Siegelkow at West-LB. "The market ignored that there was some progress in the latest talks but agreement on the stability pact should help boost the mark as it would help to ensure fiscal stability in Europe."
